paragraphs: Risk-sensitive decisions require estimates of risk together with a sense of how uncertain those estimates are. This paper develops a framework for constructing confidence bounds across several risk measures, including conditional value at risk, entropic risk, and measures that give different importance to different parts of an outcome distribution.

The central change is to handle uncertainty at the distribution level. Conventional approaches start with the risk calculated from observed data and add or subtract a confidence radius. The proposed methods instead transform the empirical distribution and evaluate risk using that transformation. Two versions use concentration bounds expressed through Wasserstein distance or supremum distance.

The authors report that these constructions produce tighter confidence bounds than previous methods. This matters because uncertainty about a distribution need not affect every risk measure in the same way. They also apply the framework to a CVaR bandit problem and obtain a tighter problem-dependent regret bound, connecting the improved statistical estimates to a guarantee for sequential decisions.
icml-2023-a-distribution-optimization-fr.tldr: Optimizing uncertainty at the distribution level yields tighter confidence bounds for several risk measures and a sharper CVaR bandit regret bound.

paragraphs: A model's accuracy on familiar data is often used to understand how it will perform on a different distribution. This paper examines that relationship when the distribution change involves subpopulations. It challenges the idea that performance on the original and shifted distributions necessarily follows an almost straight-line relationship.

Across experiments with different datasets, architectures, training durations, hyperparameters, and population imbalances, the authors find an often nonlinear relationship. Accuracy on majority and minority subpopulations traces a curved, roughly parabolic upward pattern that they call a moon shape. Consequently, a given improvement on one population does not imply a proportionally equal improvement on the other.

Controlled experiments identify the strength of spurious correlations in training data as a causal influence on this curvature: stronger spurious correlations produce greater nonlinearity. Complementary theoretical and experimental analyses investigate the phenomenon. The findings matter for reliability and fairness because they show why overall model improvement needs to be interpreted alongside its uneven relationship with performance across subpopulations.
icml-2023-accuracy-on-the-curve-on-the-n.tldr: Performance across majority and minority subpopulations often follows a nonlinear curve whose curvature increases with spurious training correlations.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate plans for offline reinforcement learning, but their planning ability depends on the diversity of their training data. AdaptDiffuser addresses this restriction by letting a planner generate additional training examples and then improve itself using selected examples. The aim is to improve familiar tasks and support adaptation to new ones.

The method uses reward gradients to guide the generation of synthetic expert data for tasks specified by a goal. A discriminator selects high-quality generated data, which is then used to fine-tune the diffusion model. This creates a feedback process linking guided generation, quality selection, and further planner training.

Experiments cover two benchmark environments and two specially designed unseen tasks in KUKA and Maze2D environments. The abstract reports improvements over Diffuser of 20.8% on Maze2D and 7.5% on MuJoCo locomotion, plus a 27.9% improvement in adaptation to KUKA pick-and-place without additional expert data. These results support the usefulness of the proposed self-improvement process in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-adaptdiffuser-diffusion-models.tldr: AdaptDiffuser improves diffusion-based planning by generating reward-guided synthetic data, selecting strong examples, and fine-tuning on them.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based art systems raise concerns when paintings are used without authorization to produce new work in a similar style. This paper investigates a technical protection strategy: creating adversarial versions of artworks that interfere with a diffusion model's ability to extract their features. The intended application is helping artists resist unauthorized imitation.

The authors first develop a theoretical framework for defining and evaluating adversarial examples specifically for diffusion models. They then introduce AdvDM, an algorithm built around Monte Carlo estimation. It optimizes over different latent variables sampled from the diffusion model's reverse process, using these samples to construct the adversarial examples.

The reported experiments show that the resulting examples can effectively hinder feature extraction by diffusion models. This gives the proposed protection a concrete technical target: disrupting the model's acquisition of information from the artwork. The findings support adversarial examples as a possible tool for protecting artists' work against diffusion-based imitation; the stated result concerns interference with model behavior rather than a universal guarantee against copying.
icml-2023-adversarial-example-does-good-.tldr: AdvDM constructs adversarial artwork examples that experimentally hinder diffusion models from extracting features used for imitation.

paragraphs: Choosing a tensor network structure can require many expensive evaluations of candidate models. This paper introduces TnALE to reduce that search cost. Its basic procedure alternates among variables describing the structure, enumerating nearby choices for one variable at a time instead of relying on the more evaluation-intensive search used by TNLS.

The analysis compares how both algorithms decrease their objective. Both can achieve linear convergence up to a constant if each neighborhood search obtains a sufficient reduction. The evaluation comparison is also qualified: TNLS typically requires at least exponentially many evaluations in the search dimension K, while TnALE ideally needs only O(KR), where R describes the neighborhood's low-rank structure.

These statements explain where the potential efficiency gain comes from while retaining the conditions behind it. Alternating local searches can exploit favorable neighborhood structure to find improvements with fewer evaluations. Experiments support the practical value of that idea: TnALE finds good tensor network structures using vastly fewer objective evaluations than the compared state-of-the-art methods.
icml-2023-alternating-local-enumeration-.tldr: TnALE searches tensor network structures through alternating local enumeration, finding good structures with far fewer evaluations in experiments.

paragraphs: Image segmentation involves grouping pixels, but different tasks ask for different kinds of groups. CLUSTSEG presents a transformer-based framework that handles superpixel, semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation through a common neural clustering procedure. Its organizing idea is to treat transformer queries as cluster centers around which pixel groups are formed.

The framework accommodates task-specific needs by initializing these centers in different ways. For example, distinguishing object instances and distinguishing categories call for different forms of distinctiveness. Those differences are handled through initialization without changing the architecture. This makes the clustering formulation a shared mechanism across the supported segmentation tasks.

CLUSTSEG then alternates between assigning pixels to clusters through cross-attention and updating the cluster centers, without learning additional parameters for this alternation. The authors connect this process to expectation-maximization clustering, making the roles of assignment and updating more explicit. They report superior results across the listed tasks, supporting the usefulness of a common clustering approach with task-sensitive initialization.
icml-2023-clustseg-clustering-for-univer.tldr: CLUSTSEG unifies several segmentation tasks by treating transformer queries as cluster centers and alternating pixel assignments with center updates.

paragraphs: Early stopping uses held-out data to decide when a neural network should stop training, helping reduce overfitting. Although this can improve prediction accuracy, accurate predictions alone do not supply precise statistical guarantees. Conformal calibration can provide predictive inference, but ordinarily requires independent held-out data beyond the examples already used to select a stopping point.

This paper introduces conformalized early stopping, which combines stopping decisions and conformal calibration while reusing the same held-out data. The contribution is a method for making that reuse statistically valid. It avoids requiring multiple data splits or relying on overly conservative adjustments to account for the shared use of data.

The authors develop practical versions for outlier detection, multiclass classification, and regression, and demonstrate competitive performance on real data. The stated outcome combines accurate models with exact predictive inference. Its practical importance lies in connecting a familiar training procedure to statistical calibration while making more efficient use of the held-out examples that the procedure already requires.
icml-2023-conformal-inference-is-almost-.tldr: Conformalized early stopping reuses held-out data for both stopping and calibration while providing exact predictive inference.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel clustering combines several kernels, making the learned weights an important part of the clustering method. This paper studies whether the weights produced by SimpleMKKM are statistically consistent. It provides finite-sample analysis, connecting the amount of available data to bounds on weight estimation and excess clustering risk.

Under eigenvalue-gap assumptions, the authors bound the maximum coordinate error of the weights at a rate of approximately k divided by the square root of n, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here k is the number of clusters and n is the sample count. They also bound the difference between weights learned from all n samples and from r points sampled without replacement.

The subsampling bound scales approximately as k times the square root of 1/r minus 1/n. These results motivate a Nyström-based strategy for applying SimpleMKKM to large datasets with a theoretical learning guarantee. Experiments examine both the theoretical predictions and the effectiveness of this scalable strategy, linking consistency analysis to a practical computational method.
icml-2023-consistency-of-multiple-kernel.tldr: Finite-sample guarantees for SimpleMKKM's kernel weights support a theoretically grounded Nyström strategy for larger datasets.

paragraphs: Zero-shot coordination asks an agent to cooperate effectively with partners it has not encountered during training. Increasing the diversity of a training population can help expose different behaviors, but diversity alone can leave agents unable to cooperate with some strategies. The paper calls this failure cooperative incompatibility.

The proposed COLE framework builds open-ended learning objectives for cooperative games involving two players. It uses a graph-theoretic perspective to assess the cooperative ability of individual strategies, then turns the framework into a practical algorithm drawing on both graph theory and game theory. The objective construction makes cooperative ability central to the learning process.

An analysis of the algorithm's learning process indicates that it can efficiently overcome cooperative incompatibility. Experiments in Overcooked show better coordination with partners at different levels than the compared state-of-the-art methods. Together, these results support adapting the objectives used to train a population so that learning addresses compatibility with different partners, rather than assuming that a diverse collection of strategies will automatically cooperate well.
icml-2023-cooperative-open-ended-learnin.tldr: COLE uses graph-informed, open-ended objectives to improve cooperation with unseen partners and address incompatible strategies.

paragraphs: Some approaches to interpreting neural networks extract interactions among input variables and describe those interactions as concepts learned by the network. This paper asks whether that description is trustworthy. Finding an interaction in a model does not, by itself, establish that the interaction corresponds to a meaningful concept.

The authors examine interaction concepts from four perspectives and conduct extensive empirical studies. Their reported finding is that well-trained deep networks usually encode concepts that are sparse, transferable, and discriminative. These properties concern how selectively concepts appear, whether they carry over, and whether they help distinguish inputs, providing several ways to assess the proposed interpretation.

The result offers empirical support for treating some learned interactions as meaningful concepts, with an explicit qualification: the observed properties align only partly with human intuition. The contribution therefore concerns the evidence behind an interpretability claim, rather than simply naming extracted patterns. Its wording also matters: the abstract describes what well-trained networks usually exhibit in empirical studies, without establishing that every extracted interaction is a human-like symbolic concept.
icml-2023-does-a-neural-network-really-e.tldr: Empirical studies find that well-trained networks usually encode sparse, transferable, discriminative interaction concepts that partly align with human intuition.

paragraphs: Designing protein structures involves three related goals: structures should be realizable by protein sequences, differ from natural protein geometries, and cover a broad range of shapes. Searching directly through the enormous space of sequences and structures is difficult. This paper develops Genie, a generative model intended to produce promising structures directly.

Genie combines denoising diffusion with equivariant neural networks. It represents a protein structure as a collection of oriented reference frames in three-dimensional space and applies a discrete-time diffusion process to that representation. The representation includes orientation as well as spatial placement, giving the model a geometric basis for generating protein backbones.

Computational evaluations show that Genie produces backbones that are more designable, novel, and diverse than those generated by existing models. The authors interpret these results as evidence that Genie captures important features of the distribution of protein structures and supports protein design with high success rates. The stated evidence comes from in silico evaluation, so the reported achievement concerns computationally assessed structure generation and designability.
icml-2023-generating-novel-designable-an.tldr: Genie uses geometric diffusion to generate protein backbones with improved designability, novelty, and diversity in computational evaluations.

paragraphs: In some reinforcement learning problems, a discriminator supplies the reward used to train a policy, and the discriminator is itself trained alongside that policy. The paper formalizes this setting as internally rewarded reinforcement learning. Its defining feature is that the learning system generates its reward internally instead of receiving it directly from the environment.

This arrangement creates a feedback problem. An immature discriminator can produce noisy rewards that obstruct policy learning, while a poorly optimized policy can obstruct discriminator learning. The authors identify a class of problems with this structure and analyze, both theoretically and empirically, how the reward function affects the resulting learning process.

Based on that analysis, they propose a clipped linear reward function. Experiments across diverse tasks show that the proposed function consistently stabilizes training by reducing the influence of reward noise, with faster convergence and higher performance than the evaluated baselines. The contribution is thus both a formulation of the coupled learning problem and a reward-design intervention supported by the reported experiments.
icml-2023-internally-rewarded-reinforcem.tldr: A clipped linear reward reduces reward-noise effects and improves training when a policy and its reward-generating discriminator learn together.

paragraphs: The order of compiler optimization passes can substantially affect program size. Learning an effective ordering is difficult when methods require many passes during compilation or fail to transfer to unfamiliar programs. This paper approaches the problem by learning to choose whole pass sequences rather than predicting the next pass repeatedly.

The authors first identify a small collection of sequences, called a coreset, that generally reduce program size across many programs. A policy then predicts normalized values for the sequences in that collection and uses those predictions to select sequences. This organizes the decision around a compact set of complete alternatives.

Across 4,683 unseen code repositories from diverse domains and 14 datasets, the method improves on the default -Oz setting by an average of 4.5%. The authors connect its effectiveness to the denser rewards available in sequence space, while individual-pass approaches may face sparse rewards and poor cross-domain generalization. The results show that better selection and ordering can improve the use of existing human-designed compiler passes.
icml-2023-learning-compiler-pass-orders-.tldr: Selecting among a small learned collection of compiler pass sequences improves program size over -Oz on diverse unseen repositories.

paragraphs: Layer-wise distillation trains a smaller language model to imitate the intermediate representations of a larger teacher. This can be difficult because the student has less capacity, while the teacher's representations include information the target task does not require. Asking the student to match all of that information can leave it under-fitted.

Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation, or TED, introduces filters that select task-relevant knowledge from intermediate representations. These filters align the student and teacher at each layer around information useful for the target task. The intended effect is to reduce the knowledge gap and make the imitation problem better matched to the student's capacity.

The authors evaluate TED in continual pre-training and fine-tuning, reporting significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both settings. The findings support a selective approach to transferring intermediate knowledge: the useful training target is shaped by the task. This explains why reducing the information a student must imitate can help it fit the target task more effectively.
icml-2023-less-is-more-task-aware-layer-.tldr: TED filters intermediate teacher and student representations for task-relevant knowledge, improving language-model distillation in two training settings.

paragraphs: Neural networks can quickly predict solutions to constrained optimization problems, but prediction errors can violate the constraints. This paper proposes a low-complexity correction method with a feasibility guarantee. Its scope is constraint sets homeomorphic to a unit ball, covering all compact convex sets and certain nonconvex classes described by the authors.

The method learns an invertible mapping between the constraint set and a unit ball, seeking to keep geometric distortion small. It then performs a simple bisection operation in relation to the ball and uses the invertible network to map the result into a feasible solution. The ball supplies a simpler geometry for enforcing feasibility.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove feasibility and bound the optimality loss caused by distortion. Simulations include nonconvex alternating-current optimal power flow problems in power grids. They show better feasibility and runtime complexity than existing methods, with similar optimality loss. The result ties the speed of neural solution prediction to a correction procedure whose guarantees depend on the stated geometric setting and conditions.
icml-2023-low-complexity-homeomorphic-pr.tldr: An invertible mapping to a unit ball enables efficient correction of neural optimization outputs with conditional feasibility and optimality-loss guarantees.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves variables working toward opposing objectives: one side minimizes while the other maximizes. This paper studies separable convex-concave problems, where individual components can be distinguished from the component coupling the two sides. It introduces AcceleratedGradient-OptimisticGradient descent ascent, or AG-OG, to exploit that structure.

AG-OG applies Nesterov acceleration to the individual component and optimistic gradient updates to the coupling component. With appropriate restarting, the authors prove convergence rates that are optimal up to a constant across several settings. These include bilinearly coupled strongly convex–strongly concave problems, convex–strongly concave problems, and bilinear games.

The method also extends to stochastic optimization, achieving optimal rates in the two stated bilinearly coupled convexity settings. The authors identify AG-OG as the first single-call algorithm with optimal convergence rates in both deterministic and stochastic bilinearly coupled minimax optimization. The significance is that matching different update mechanisms to different parts of the objective delivers strong rate guarantees within the analyzed problem classes.
icml-2023-nesterov-meets-optimism-rate-o.tldr: AG-OG combines acceleration and optimistic gradients to attain optimal convergence rates in several structured minimax settings.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning improves a policy using previously collected transitions. One successful approach maximizes a learned value function while keeping the new policy close to the behavior that generated the data. That constraint limits distributional shift, reducing the mismatch between the data available for learning and the actions selected by the improved policy.

This paper observes that the behavior constraint naturally motivates a first-order Taylor approximation of the policy objective. The resulting linear approximation helps make policy improvement analytically tractable. To represent datasets collected by heterogeneous policies, the authors model behavior using a Gaussian mixture, then use a LogSumExp lower bound and Jensen's inequality to handle the resulting optimization difficulties.

These steps produce closed-form policy improvement operators, which the authors incorporate into both one-step and iterative offline learning algorithms. Experiments on D4RL demonstrate their effectiveness compared with state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution connects an existing constraint on behavioral change to an approximation and mixture-model treatment that yields explicit policy updates.
icml-2023-offline-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Behavior-constrained approximations and Gaussian mixture modeling yield closed-form policy improvement operators for offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Best arm identification studies how sequential interactions can reveal the best decision among candidates. This paper introduces Optimal Arms identification with Knapsacks, or OAK, to incorporate resource consumption into that exploration problem. Resource constraints make the structure of feasible decisions part of what an identification algorithm must account for.

The authors propose an OAK algorithm and analyze its probability bound by connecting optimal action selection to the geometry of the feasible region. They introduce a new complexity measure that expresses the difficulty of the problem and links this identification setting with bandits with knapsacks. This measure supports analysis of both achievable performance and fundamental difficulty.

An instance-dependent lower bound provides a reference for evaluating the algorithm's upper bound. Together, the results establish a near-optimal probability bound for OAK. For several special cases, including simple OAK and some classical pure exploration problems, the algorithm recovers or improves existing upper bounds. The framework therefore extends resource-aware identification while retaining useful connections to established exploration problems.
icml-2023-optimal-arms-identification-wi.tldr: OAK extends best arm identification to resource constraints and provides an algorithm with a near-optimal probability bound.

paragraphs: Domain randomization trains reinforcement learning agents across varied simulator parameters to improve transfer to reality. Its reach is restricted by the details a simulator can represent and by assumptions about how those parameters are distributed. Even a complex simulator has a finite parameterization and simplified physical models.

This paper reinterprets domain randomization through adversarial perturbations of states. The proposed approach does not require reconfiguring the simulator or supplying prior knowledge of the environment. It also addresses a drawback of purely worst-case perturbations: training against the worst states can make an agent overly conservative.

The Relaxed State-Adversarial Algorithm therefore simultaneously maximizes average-case and worst-case returns. This objective incorporates both ordinary performance and performance under difficult perturbations into training. The authors provide theoretical proofs and experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art methods to support its effectiveness. The contribution is a different route to robustness, built around state perturbations and a relaxed adversarial objective rather than relying exclusively on distributions over simulator parameters.
icml-2023-revisiting-domain-randomizatio.tldr: Relaxed adversarial state perturbations combine average-case and worst-case objectives to address limitations of simulator-based domain randomization.

paragraphs: In large first-price auction markets, buyers may manage budgets through pacing, creating market behavior described by first-price pacing equilibria. This paper develops statistical inference for that setting, motivated by advertising auctions. The goal is to estimate long-run market quantities and support statistically valid comparisons of changes to an auction platform.

The framework distinguishes a limiting market with a continuum of items from an observed market with finitely many items. The limiting equilibrium represents long-run steady-state behavior, while the finite equilibrium supplies data for estimation. Quantities of interest include revenue and Nash social welfare, an efficiency measure incorporating fairness.

The authors derive central limit theorems and confidence intervals that are valid asymptotically. They also establish asymptotic local minimax optimality of the estimators and show how the theory supports A/B testing. Numerical simulations agree with the predicted limiting distributions and confidence-interval coverage. The guarantees concern asymptotic inference, connecting finite observed auction data to estimates of the underlying long-run equilibrium.
icml-2023-statistical-inference-and-a-b-.tldr: A statistical framework for budget-paced first-price auctions provides asymptotic confidence intervals and supports valid A/B testing.

paragraphs: Devices with limited local data can benefit from learning together, but different devices may need personalized models for different tasks. Structured Cooperative Learning, or SCooL, addresses how to organize that cooperation. It uses a graphical model prior to generate a graph describing mutual learning relationships among devices.

Different choices of graph-generating structure produce a family of decentralized learning algorithms through variational inference. The paper presents three versions based on a Dirac distribution, a stochastic block model, and attention. Their expectation-maximization-style procedures alternate between updating the cooperation graph and cooperatively training the local models.

The algorithms infer relationships between tasks by monitoring model updates, using that information to improve the cooperation graph. Across the extensive benchmarks reported in the abstract, SCooL achieves the highest personalized-model accuracy and significantly better communication efficiency than the compared methods. These results support learning the pattern of cooperation alongside the models themselves, so that the sharing structure reflects the relationships among devices' tasks.
icml-2023-structured-cooperative-learnin.tldr: SCooL learns cooperation graphs alongside personalized device models, improving accuracy and communication efficiency on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Metric learning for image retrieval aims to arrange representations so that relevant images rank ahead of irrelevant ones. Many training losses focus on matching the labeled ranking, but semantically inconsistent labels can encourage overfitting. These methods can also depend on having a large amount of training data.

The paper introduces contextual loss, which optimizes contextual similarity together with cosine similarity. It implicitly encourages semantic consistency among neighboring samples while converging toward the correct ranking. The approach makes the relationships around an example part of the learning objective, supplementing the direct similarity information used to order individual samples.

Experiments show greater robustness to label noise and less tendency to overfit when a large portion of the training set is withheld. The method also reaches a new state of the art across four image retrieval benchmarks and multiple evaluation settings. These findings support neighborhood consistency as a useful training signal when labels are imperfect or data is limited, while retaining the central retrieval goal of learning an effective ranking.
icml-2023-supervised-metric-learning-to-.tldr: Contextual loss adds neighborhood consistency to image retrieval training, improving measured robustness to noisy labels and reduced training data.

paragraphs: A policy that improves average outcomes for a subgroup can still negatively affect some individuals. This paper focuses on that distinction by formalizing a counterfactual no-harm criterion for treatment policies. It uses a principal stratification perspective to express individual-level harm in terms of counterfactual outcomes.

The authors propose an upper bound on the fraction of people negatively affected by a policy. They establish consistency and asymptotic normality for its estimator, giving a statistical basis for assessing the bound. Policy learning then uses estimates of both utility and the harm upper bound, bringing the no-harm criterion into the optimization process.

For parametric and nonparametric policy classes, the paper proves consistency toward the optimal policy reward for the proposed approach. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in satisfying the counterfactual no-harm criterion. The contribution connects an individual-focused definition of harm to estimable population quantities and a policy-learning method, rather than treating good average utility as sufficient evidence of harmless decisions.
icml-2023-trustworthy-policy-learning-un.tldr: The paper learns policies using utility estimates and an estimated upper bound on individual counterfactual harm.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can be difficult when rewards provide little guidance toward successful behavior. A common response is to design explicit exploration strategies. This paper studies another possibility: introduce easier related tasks so that solving them in sequence provides a curriculum for the original difficult task.

The authors give a theoretical framework that reformulates a single-task problem as a multitask problem defined by such a curriculum. Under mild regularity conditions on the curriculum, sequentially solving its tasks is more computationally efficient than solving the original task from scratch. This advantage does not require explicit exploration bonuses or other exploration strategies.

The conditions on the curriculum are central to the claim: the result identifies a setting where a structured sequence of tasks provides a computational benefit. The authors also translate their theoretical insights into a practical algorithm that accelerates curriculum learning on simulated robotic tasks. Together, the analysis and experiments explain how reformulating the learning problem can improve efficiency without adding a dedicated exploration mechanism.
icml-2023-understanding-the-complexity-g.tldr: Under curriculum regularity conditions, solving easier tasks sequentially reduces the computational cost of learning a difficult reinforcement learning task.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented models combine a retriever with a model that uses retrieved information to answer questions or model language. This paper introduces Variational Open-Domain, or VOD, as a framework for training and evaluating these components end to end. Its focus is optimizing retrieval-augmented systems through variational inference.

The objective approximates the task's marginal likelihood using a self-normalized estimate of a Rényi variational bound. It is evaluated with samples from an auxiliary distribution, such as a cached retriever or an approximate posterior. This sampling construction keeps the objective tractable even when the retriever assigns probabilities over a large document collection.

The authors train BERT-sized reader-retriever systems on multiple-choice medical exam questions. Their retrieval-augmented BioLinkBERT scores 62.9% on MedMCQA and 55.0% on MedQA-USMLE; the abstract reports a +5.3% advantage over domain-tuned Med-PaLM on MedMCQA with 2,500 times fewer parameters. They also demonstrate the learned retriever's effectiveness for medical semantic search, showing value in both the combined answering system and its retrieval component.
icml-2023-variational-open-domain-questi.tldr: VOD makes variational training of retrieval-augmented models tractable over large corpora and demonstrates strong medical question-answering results.
